Tables, figures and text

Source: vignettes/v03-tables-figures-text.Rmd
v03-tables-figures-text.Rmd
library(pubflow)
library(ggplot2)

Get started built a table, a figure and a text in three steps of a pipeline. This vignette looks at these outputs in turn: what they are, how you set them up and how the pieces of a document refer to each other. The steps that return them are ordinary pipeflow steps (see pipeflow’s Get started); the vignette on documents and layout steps shows how to arrange the outputs into a document.

An output is a plain R object with metadata: a table is a huxtable, a figure a ggplot or a recorded plot, a text a character string. Functions that read the object, e.g. print() or summary(), work as on the object without the metadata.

The examples show outputs one at a time, each as a small document rendered to HTML. They use this helper:

show_doc <- function(...) pub_html(pub_doc(...))

Tables

pub_table() builds a table from a data.frame. We summarise the ozone concentration of New York in airquality by month:

monthly <- aggregate(Ozone ~ Month, data = airquality, FUN = function(x) {
    c(n = length(x), mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x))
}) |>
    do.call(what = data.frame)
names(monthly) <- c("month", "n", "mean", "sd")
monthly$n <- as.integer(monthly$n)
monthly$month <- month.name[monthly$month]
monthly
#       month  n     mean       sd
# 1       May 26 23.61538 22.22445
# 2      June  9 29.44444 18.20790
# 3      July 26 59.11538 31.63584
# 4    August 26 59.96154 39.68121
# 5 September 29 31.44828 24.14182

A table gets a caption, readable column labels and the number of decimal places of the numeric columns:

tab <- pub_table(
    monthly,
    caption = "Ozone concentration by month",
    labels = c(month = "Month", n = "N", mean = "Mean (ppb)", sd = "SD (ppb)"),
    digits = c(mean = 1L, sd = 1L)
)
show_doc(tab)
Table 1: Ozone concentration by month
Month N Mean (ppb) SD (ppb)
May 26 23.6 22.2
June 9 29.4 18.2
July 26 59.1 31.6
August 26 60.0 39.7
September 29 31.4 24.1

Columns without digits get the number format of the table theme (four decimal places by default), and whole numbers like n get none.

The result is a huxtable and can be used as such. pub_table() only sets it up: a header and body, a theme and the number formats. The cells keep the values and are formatted when the table is rendered, by the same code for every format (HTML, Word, PDF), so that a table shows the same text everywhere. pub_cell_text() returns this text:

pub_cell_text(tab)
#      [,1]        [,2] [,3]         [,4]      
# [1,] "Month"     "N"  "Mean (ppb)" "SD (ppb)"
# [2,] "May"       "26" "23.6"       "22.2"    
# [3,] "June"      "9"  "29.4"       "18.2"    
# [4,] "July"      "26" "59.1"       "31.6"    
# [5,] "August"    "26" "60.0"       "39.7"    
# [6,] "September" "29" "31.4"       "24.1"

Headers, footnotes and merged cells

More arguments structure the table: header puts a spanner above columns with equal labels, footnotes adds numbered footnotes below the table, merge joins consecutive equal cells of a column and na is the text for missing values. Here the data are the coefficients of a linear model of the ozone concentration, one fit per month:

fits <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(airquality, airquality$Month), function(d) {
    fit <- lm(Ozone ~ Temp, data = d)
    ci <- confint(fit)
    data.frame(
        month = month.name[d$Month[1L]],
        term = c("Intercept", "Temp"),
        estimate = coef(fit),
        lower = ci[, 1L],
        upper = ci[, 2L]
    )
}))
fits <- fits[fits$month %in% c("May", "June"), ]

pub_table(
    fits,
    caption = "Linear model of ozone by temperature",
    labels = c(
        month = "Month",
        term = "Term",
        estimate = "Estimate",
        lower = "Lower",
        upper = "Upper"
    ),
    digits = c(estimate = 2L, lower = 2L, upper = 2L),
    header = c(lower = "95% CI", upper = "95% CI"),
    footnotes = c(estimate = "Least squares fit, one per month."),
    merge = "month"
) |>
    show_doc()
Table 1: Linear model of ozone by temperature
95% CI
Month Term Estimate¹ Lower Upper
May Intercept -102.16 -182.14 -22.18
Temp 1.88 0.69 3.08
June Intercept -91.99 -213.32 29.34
Temp 1.55 0.01 3.10
¹ Least squares fit, one per month.

?pub_table lists the other arguments: alignment, column widths, font size and the table theme. A theme sets font size, borders and the default number format for all tables. Use options(pubflow.table_theme = pub_table_theme(...)) to change it for the whole session.

Style cells with huxtable

pubflow has no functions of its own to style cells, use huxtable’s, e.g. set_bold(), set_text_color() or the mapping functions like map_text_color(). Two things to keep in mind:

  • The rows of huxtable’s functions include the header rows, so the body row i is the table row sum(huxtable::header_rows(tab)) + i.
  • Give rows as integer indices (or names), not as a logical vector: huxtable recycles a short logical vector, also into the footnote rows.

Here the months with a mean above 40 ppb are set in bold red:

nHeader <- sum(huxtable::header_rows(tab))
high <- which(monthly$mean > 40)

tab |>
    huxtable::set_bold(nHeader + high, huxtable::everywhere) |>
    huxtable::set_text_color(nHeader + high, huxtable::everywhere, "darkred") |>
    show_doc()
Table 1: Ozone concentration by month
Month N Mean (ppb) SD (ppb)
May 26 23.6 22.2
June 9 29.4 18.2
July 26 59.1 31.6
August 26 60.0 39.7
September 29 31.4 24.1

Call huxtable’s functions with the huxtable:: prefix, as other packages (flextable) mask some of their names.

Struck-through cells

pub_strikeout() strikes cells through, e.g. for excluded measurements. It shows the text of the cells as they are formatted, so strike through last, after all number formats are set:

runs <- data.frame(
    sample = c("S1", "S2", "S3"),
    result = c(0.8, 12.25, 0.95),
    excluded = c(FALSE, TRUE, FALSE)
)
tabRuns <- pub_table(
    runs[, c("sample", "result")],
    caption = "Assay results",
    digits = c(result = 2L)
)
rows <- sum(huxtable::header_rows(tabRuns)) + which(runs$excluded)
tabRuns |>
    huxtable::set_text_color(rows, huxtable::everywhere, "grey50") |>
    pub_strikeout(rows) |>
    show_doc()
Table 1: Assay results
sample result
S1 0.80

S2

12.25
S3 0.95

Word, PDF and HTML all show the cells struck through. There is no underline.

Combining tables

Combine the data and build the table once, rather than gluing finished tables together: bind the data of several batches with rbind() and give pub_table(merge = "batch"), or subset the data to get one table per batch.

If you do combine finished tables with huxtable’s rbind(), cbind() or [, the cell styles are kept, but the pieces are bound by position, each keeps its own borders and the metadata of the table (see below) get lost, except for rbind(), which keeps those of the first table. Finish the result with pub_table() again and set the footnotes, widths and metadata on the final table.

Rounding

Numbers in tables are rounded half away from zero on their decimal text, as in the USP General Notices (7.20) and SAS’s ROUND(): if the first dropped digit is 5 or more, the last digit goes up. R’s round(), sprintf() and formatC() round the binary value instead and send exact ties to the even digit:

x <- c(0.125, 2.675, -2.675, 9.995)
round(x, 2)
# [1]  0.12  2.67 -2.67  9.99
pub_round(x, 2)
# [1]  0.13  2.68 -2.68 10.00

Use the same rules wherever a number appears outside a table. pub_round() returns the rounded numbers, e.g. to compare a result with a limit that is specified with a number of decimal places. pub_format_num() returns the text that a table cell would show, so you can quote a number in a text and it matches the table:

pub_format_num(x, 2)
# [1] "0.13"  "2.68"  "-2.68" "10.00"
pub_format_num(mean(c(98.25, 99.1)), "Mean assay: %.2f %%")
# [1] "Mean assay: 98.68 %"

A format is a number of decimal places or a sprintf() format with exactly one %.nf, %.ne or %.ng conversion (?pub_round). The number_format of a table theme accepts the same; digits of pub_table() takes decimal places only.

Figures

A plot is a figure without further ado: a ggplot or a recorded base plot (grDevices::recordPlot()) in a document is shown as a figure. pub_figure() adds a caption, a size or other metadata. Image files need it, as otherwise their paths would be taken as text:

trend_plot <- function(data) {
    p <- ggplot(data, aes(.data$Temp, .data$Ozone)) +
        geom_point(na.rm = TRUE) +
        geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, na.rm = TRUE)
    pub_figure(
        p,
        caption = "Ozone concentration by temperature",
        width = 6,
        height = 3.5
    )
}
fig <- trend_plot(airquality)
show_doc(fig)

The size is in inches (default 8 x 6) and sets the proportions of the plot in the document; out_width = "60%" shrinks the figure relative to the text width.

As in Get started, the function that makes the plot is defined outside the pipeline: a ggplot keeps the environment it was made in, so a plot made by code inside a pipeline’s constructor would hold the whole pipeline in every copy.

Image files, e.g. made by another program, are figures too. Give one file, or several files of the same plot, e.g. a png and a pdf. Each output format takes the file that suits it: HTML and Word show the png (or jpg), a PDF made with LaTeX can use the vector file (see ?pub_figure).

pub_figure(c("trend.png", "trend.pdf"), caption = "Trend")

Figures rendered in the step

Usually a plot is drawn when the document is rendered. With render = TRUE, pub_figure() draws it right away, at its size and 200 dpi, and returns the png image with the metadata:

png <- pub_figure(fig, render = TRUE)
png
# <pubflow figure> PNG 1200 x 700 px (6 x 3.5 in, 200 dpi), 60 KB
# Caption: Ozone concentration by temperature
pub_type(png)
# [1] "figure"

Use it in steps that run in other R processes (workers) and for pipelines that are saved with saveRDS(). A ggplot holds environments, so a copy of it is no longer identical to the original, and the document draws it again although nothing changed. The image survives copying unchanged, so the document uses it as it is:

identical(fig, unserialize(serialize(fig, NULL)))
# [1] FALSE
identical(png, unserialize(serialize(png, NULL)))
# [1] TRUE

Recorded base plots need it too, as they can’t be replayed in another R session. The price: the image can’t be changed by later steps, so the step that renders it should be the last that touches the figure, and its size is fixed (use out_width to scale it in the document). A report with vector figures (figure = list(device = "pdf")) still shows the png. Caption, id and other metadata can be set as for any figure:

show_doc(pub_figure(png, caption = "Ozone concentration by temperature (rendered)"))

Texts

A text is a character vector in Markdown. pub_text() joins the lines and checks the Markdown:

txt <- pub_text(
    c(
        "The model explains **49%** of the variance ($R^2 = 0.49$).",
        "",
        "- the data are from May to September 1973",
        "- missing ozone values are left out",
        "",
        "Complete the discussion: [<insert text>]{.placeholder}"
    ),
    title = "Summary"
)
show_doc(txt)
Summary

The model explains 49% of the variance (\(R^2 = 0.49\)).

  • the data are from May to September 1973
  • missing ozone values are left out

Complete the discussion: <insert text>

The supported Markdown is the same in all formats: paragraphs, emphasis, code, links, bullet and numbered lists, line breaks, inline and display math and code blocks. A placeholder ([<insert text>]{.placeholder}) marks a gap that someone fills in by hand, e.g. in the Word report. It is highlighted in every format. A heading is an error, as the structure of a document comes from its sections (see the vignette on documents and layout steps):

pub_text(c("# Results", "Some text"))
# Error in `pub_text()`:
# ! Text must not contain headings (use sections):
# ✖ line 1: "# Results"

Format numbers in a text with pub_format_num() (see above), so that they agree with the tables. A step can also return a plain character vector, which is checked in the same way when it is put into a document.

Metadata

Each output carries metadata, a named list in the attribute pubflow. pub_table(), pub_figure() and pub_text() set it for you, and pub_meta() reads it:

pub_type(fig)
# [1] "figure"
pub_meta(fig)
# $caption
# [1] "Ozone concentration by temperature"
# 
# $width
# [1] 6
# 
# $height
# [1] 3.5
pub_meta(tab, "caption")
# [1] "Ozone concentration by month"

pub_type() tells what a document makes of an object: a table, figure, text or a few other types. pub_set_meta() sets or removes single entries, e.g. a title that is shown above the item, landscape = TRUE to place it on landscape pages (Word and PDF) or locked = TRUE to lock it in Word against accidental edits. Keys that pubflow doesn’t know are kept, so you can add your own.

tab <- pub_set_meta(tab, title = "Monthly summary", id = "monthly")
pub_meta(tab)
# $title
# [1] "Monthly summary"
# 
# $id
# [1] "monthly"
# 
# $caption
# [1] "Ozone concentration by month"

The metadata of a huxtable are kept by rbind(), but not by [ and cbind(), see Combining tables. ?pub_meta lists the keys.

Cross-references

A text can refer to a table or figure: @tab:<id> and @fig:<id> stand for “Table 1” or “Figure 2” and link to the item with that id in its metadata. The item needs a caption, as only captions are numbered, and its id must be unique in the document. The ids start with a letter, end with a letter or digit and contain only letters, digits, _ and -:

fig <- pub_set_meta(fig, id = "trend")

txt <- pub_text(c(
    "@tab:monthly lists the ozone concentration by month, @fig:trend shows",
    "how it depends on the temperature."
))
show_doc(txt, tab, fig)

Table 1 lists the ozone concentration by month, Figure 1 shows how it depends on the temperature.

Monthly summary
Table 1: Ozone concentration by month
Month N Mean (ppb) SD (ppb)
May 26 23.6 22.2
June 9 29.4 18.2
July 26 59.1 31.6
August 26 60.0 39.7
September 29 31.4 24.1

In a Word report these are cross-reference fields, in LaTeX and Typst references, in HTML links, and the numbering is the engine’s own. So the numbers stay right when someone moves a figure in Word and updates the fields. The word before the number (“Table”, “Figure”) comes from the labels of the report spec (see ?pub_report_spec). Only texts contain references; captions, titles and table cells show @fig:x as it is. Text in code, math, placeholders and links is left alone, as are \@fig:x and a@fig:x.

A reference that can’t be resolved (unknown id, missing caption, a duplicate id) is an error when you write a report with pub_render(), listing all problems, so that a broken reference never goes unnoticed. pub_html() and the viewer only warn and show the reference as marked text, so that a draft still displays:

broken <- pub_text("See @fig:missing.")
html <- pub_html(pub_doc(broken))
# Warning: Can't resolve the cross-references of the document.
# ✖ `@fig:missing`: no table or figure has the id 'missing'.
# ℹ References (`@fig:<id>`, `@tab:<id>`) need one captioned item with the id.
